title: The Strength of Weak Ties
body:
Common sense suggests that the people who help us most are the people who know us best. A study of how professional men in a Boston suburb had found their jobs produced the opposite result. Those who learned of an opening through a personal contact had usually heard it not from a close friend or relative but from someone they saw rarely, in several cases someone they had nearly forgotten. The finding was counterintuitive enough to require an explanation, and the explanation reshaped how sociologists think about the architecture of a society. It also inverted a long habit of treating intimacy as the measure of a relationship's worth, since it implied that the bonds a person values least may be the ones doing the most consequential work.

The argument turns on redundancy. Close friends tend to move in the same circle as we do, attend the same gatherings, and read the same notices. Whatever reaches them is therefore likely to reach us anyway, and often has already. An acquaintance seen twice a year belongs to a different circle, and the information circulating there is genuinely new. The value of a relationship as a channel depends less on its warmth than on the distance it spans, and casual ties tend to span the greater distance precisely because they are casual.

The consequences extend well beyond employment. If a community is divided into dense clusters whose members all know one another, then anything that must travel between clusters, whether a rumor, a technique, or a contagion, can cross only along the sparse links that connect them. Remove those links and the clusters become islands. The same geometry that makes a bridging tie valuable also makes it fragile, for a connection maintained by neither habit nor affection is the first to lapse when either party grows busy. A society composed entirely of intimate bonds would be, paradoxically, a society through which very little could move, and researchers studying the spread of innovations have repeatedly found that adoption stalls where such bridging connections are absent.

The practical implications are less comfortable than they first appear. Because weak ties are cheap to maintain, one might conclude that anyone can accumulate them freely, but the circles a person can reach are constrained by where that person already stands. Studies of urban poverty have found that residents of isolated neighborhoods are not deficient in social connection; their networks are often unusually dense. What they lack is the sparse, outward-reaching kind, and the resulting disadvantage compounds, since the contacts that would carry news of opportunity are exactly the contacts that isolation prevents. Programs designed on the assumption that such communities need more solidarity may therefore address a problem that does not exist while neglecting the one that does.

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, why is information from a close friend often less useful?

choices.A: Close friends usually belong to the same circle and so know much the same things
choices.B: Close friends tend to give advice rather than concrete information
choices.C: Close friends are contacted too infrequently to be reached in time
choices.D: Close friends are reluctant to share news that might create competition

questions.explanation: 第2段落に "Close friends tend to move in the same circle as we do... Whatever reaches them is therefore likely to reach us anyway" とあり、情報が重複することが理由である。Bの助言の性質とDの競争心は本文に記述がなく、Cは close friends ではなく acquaintance の説明と混同している。

questions.question: The word "sparse" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: "dense clusters" と対置され、クラスター間をつなぐ数少ない結びつきを指している。直後の "Remove those links and the clusters become islands" も、その数が限られていることを前提にした記述である。したがって D が最も近い。Cの「維持が難しい」は次の文の fragile が述べる別の性質であって、sparse の語義ではない。

questions.question: The word "they" in paragraph 2 ("precisely because they are casual") refers to

choices.A: the circles that acquaintances belong to
choices.C: the notices that close friends read

questions.explanation: 当該文は "casual ties tend to span the greater distance precisely because they are casual" であり、casual であるのは ties 自身である。Dの distance は they が span する対象であって主語ではない。

questions.question: Why does the author mention rumors, techniques, and contagions in paragraph 3?

choices.A: To compare the speed at which different kinds of information travel
choices.B: To identify the three subjects that sociologists most often study
choices.C: To show that the same structural principle governs many different kinds of spread
choices.D: To warn that weak ties can spread harmful things as well as useful ones

questions.explanation: 三つは "anything that must travel between clusters" の例として並置されており、いずれもクラスター間を結ぶ疎な結びつきを通らねばならないという同一の構造的制約を示すために挙げられている。Aの速度比較は行われておらず、Bのような研究分野の列挙でもない。Dの警告は本文の主眼ではなく、contagion は構造が内容の善悪を選ばないことを示す一例にすぎない。

questions.question: It can be inferred from paragraph 4 that a program aimed at strengthening bonds within an isolated neighborhood would probably

choices.A: reduce the density of the networks that already exist there
choices.B: be resisted by residents who prefer their existing networks
choices.C: succeed only if residents were first relocated elsewhere
choices.D: fail to supply the outward connections that residents actually lack

questions.explanation: 本文は住民の網が "often unusually dense" であり、欠けているのは "the sparse, outward-reaching kind" だと述べる。したがって内部の結束を強める施策は不足分を補わない。最終文の "address a problem that does not exist while neglecting the one that does" がこの推論を裏づける。BとCは本文に根拠がなく、Aは結束を強める施策の効果として逆である。

suburb.etymology: ラテン語 sub-(下に、近くに) + urbs(都市) → suburbium「都市の周縁」
suburb.usage_in_passage: "professional men in a Boston suburb" が調査対象を特定し、都市部の貧困を扱う第4段落との社会階層の対比を暗に用意する。
suburb.context_sentence: A study of how professional men in a Boston suburb had found their jobs produced the opposite result.

opposite.etymology: ラテン語 ob-(に対して) + ponere(置く) → oppositus
opposite.usage_in_passage: "produced the opposite result" が、冒頭の常識的な想定が実証によって覆されたことを示し、本文の出発点を作る。
opposite.context_sentence: A study of how professional men in a Boston suburb had found their jobs produced the opposite result.

rarely.etymology: 古ノルド語由来の rare + -ly
rarely.usage_in_passage: "someone they saw rarely" が弱い紐帯の定義を接触頻度で与え、以降の議論の土台になる。
rarely.context_sentence: Those who learned of an opening through a personal contact had usually heard it not from a close friend or relative but from someone they saw rarely, in several cases someone they had nearly forgotten.

forgotten.etymology: 古英語 forgietan(忘れる)の過去分詞。ゲルマン系
forgotten.usage_in_passage: "someone they had nearly forgotten" が発見の意外性を極端な例で示し、counterintuitive という次の語を準備する。
forgotten.context_sentence: Those who learned of an opening through a personal contact had usually heard it not from a close friend or relative but from someone they saw rarely, in several cases someone they had nearly forgotten.

counterintuitive.etymology: counter-(反して) + ラテン語 intueri(見つめる) → intuitive の否定的複合
counterintuitive.usage_in_passage: "counterintuitive enough to require an explanation" が、この発見が説明を要する理由を述べ、第2段落の理論的説明へ橋渡しする。
counterintuitive.context_sentence: The finding was counterintuitive enough to require an explanation, and the explanation reshaped how sociologists think about the architecture of a society.

explanation.etymology: ラテン語 ex-(外に) + planus(平らな) → explanare「平らにして示す」+ -ation
explanation.usage_in_passage: 同一文で二度用いられ、説明が求められたことと、その説明が学問を変えたことを一文で結ぶ。
explanation.context_sentence: The finding was counterintuitive enough to require an explanation, and the explanation reshaped how sociologists think about the architecture of a society.

reshaped.etymology: re-(再び) + shape(古英語 sceppan)。ゲルマン系 + -ed
reshaped.usage_in_passage: "reshaped how sociologists think about the architecture of a society" が、個別の発見が理論全体に及ぼした影響の大きさを示す。
reshaped.context_sentence: The finding was counterintuitive enough to require an explanation, and the explanation reshaped how sociologists think about the architecture of a society.

sociologists.etymology: ラテン語 socius(仲間) + ギリシャ語 -logia(学問) + -ist + -s
sociologists.usage_in_passage: この知見の受け手を特定し、議論が学術的な文脈に属することを示す。
sociologists.context_sentence: The finding was counterintuitive enough to require an explanation, and the explanation reshaped how sociologists think about the architecture of a society.

inverted.etymology: ラテン語 in-(中へ) + vertere(回す) → invertere「ひっくり返す」
inverted.usage_in_passage: "It also inverted a long habit of treating intimacy as the measure" が、発見の影響が事実の訂正にとどまらず価値尺度の転倒に及ぶことを示す。
inverted.context_sentence: It also inverted a long habit of treating intimacy as the measure of a relationship's worth, since it implied that the bonds a person values least may be the ones doing the most consequential work.

habit.etymology: ラテン語 habere(持つ) → habitus「身についたもの」
habit.usage_in_passage: ここでは思考の習慣を指し、個人の癖ではなく学問的な前提の意で用いられている。
habit.context_sentence: It also inverted a long habit of treating intimacy as the measure of a relationship's worth, since it implied that the bonds a person values least may be the ones doing the most consequential work.

treating.etymology: ラテン語 tractare(扱う) < trahere(引く) + -ing
treating.usage_in_passage: "treating intimacy as the measure of a relationship's worth" が、転倒される前の従来の見方を定式化する。
treating.context_sentence: It also inverted a long habit of treating intimacy as the measure of a relationship's worth, since it implied that the bonds a person values least may be the ones doing the most consequential work.

intimacy.etymology: ラテン語 intimus(最も内side の) → intimate + -acy
intimacy.usage_in_passage: 本文が価値の尺度から外す当のもので、第3段落の "intimate bonds" と呼応する。
intimacy.context_sentence: It also inverted a long habit of treating intimacy as the measure of a relationship's worth, since it implied that the bonds a person values least may be the ones doing the most consequential work.

relationship's.etymology: relation(< ラテン語 referre 関係づける) + -ship + 所有の -'s
relationship's.usage_in_passage: "a relationship's worth" が、評価の対象を人ではなく関係そのものに定める。
relationship's.context_sentence: It also inverted a long habit of treating intimacy as the measure of a relationship's worth, since it implied that the bonds a person values least may be the ones doing the most consequential work.

implied.etymology: ラテン語 in-(中に) + plicare(折る) → implicare「含み込む」
implied.usage_in_passage: 発見が明言していないことまで導くという論理関係を示し、次の節を推論として位置づける。
implied.context_sentence: It also inverted a long habit of treating intimacy as the measure of a relationship's worth, since it implied that the bonds a person values least may be the ones doing the most consequential work.

bonds.etymology: 中英語 band「縛るもの」。bind と同系のゲルマン語 + -s
bonds.usage_in_passage: 第1段落では "the bonds a person values least"、第3段落では "intimate bonds" として現れ、本文の中心語である ties の言い換えとして機能する。
bonds.context_sentence: It also inverted a long habit of treating intimacy as the measure of a relationship's worth, since it implied that the bonds a person values least may be the ones doing the most consequential work.

consequential.etymology: ラテン語 con-(共に) + sequi(従う) + -ential
consequential.usage_in_passage: "doing the most consequential work" が、価値が低いと見なされる関係こそ効果が大きいという逆説を締めくくる。
consequential.context_sentence: It also inverted a long habit of treating intimacy as the measure of a relationship's worth, since it implied that the bonds a person values least may be the ones doing the most consequential work.

redundancy.etymology: ラテン語 re-(再び) + undare(波打つ) → redundare「あふれる」+ -ancy
redundancy.usage_in_passage: "The argument turns on redundancy" が第2段落の主題語で、なぜ親しい相手の情報が役立たないのかを一語で説明する。

tend.etymology: ラテン語 tendere(伸ばす、向かう)
tend.usage_in_passage: "Close friends tend to move in the same circle" が、断定ではなく傾向として述べることで例外の存在を認めつつ議論を進める。
tend.context_sentence: Close friends tend to move in the same circle as we do, attend the same gatherings, and read the same notices.

circle.etymology: ラテン語 circus(輪)の縮小形 circulus
circle.usage_in_passage: 本文の鍵となる比喩。同一の circle にいるかどうかが情報の新しさを決めるという構造を作る。
circle.context_sentence: Close friends tend to move in the same circle as we do, attend the same gatherings, and read the same notices.

attend.etymology: ラテン語 ad-(に) + tendere(向ける) → attendere
attend.usage_in_passage: 同じ集まりに出るという具体例で、circle の共有が何を意味するかを示す。
attend.context_sentence: Close friends tend to move in the same circle as we do, attend the same gatherings, and read the same notices.

gatherings.etymology: 古英語 gaderian(集める) → gather + -ing + -s。ゲルマン系
gatherings.usage_in_passage: 情報が流通する場を指し、同席することが情報の重複を生む経路であることを示す。
gatherings.context_sentence: Close friends tend to move in the same circle as we do, attend the same gatherings, and read the same notices.

anyway.etymology: any + way。ゲルマン系の複合語
anyway.definition: どのみち、いずれにせよ。
anyway.usage_in_passage: "likely to reach us anyway" が、親しい相手を経由する情報の限界価値がゼロに近いことを口語的に言い切る。
anyway.context_sentence: Whatever reaches them is therefore likely to reach us anyway, and often has already.

acquaintance.etymology: ラテン語 ad-(に) + cognoscere(知る) → 古フランス語 acointer + -ance
acquaintance.definition: 知人。親しい友人ではない知り合い。
acquaintance.usage_in_passage: "An acquaintance seen twice a year" が弱い紐帯を人物として具体化し、close friend との対比を完成させる。
acquaintance.context_sentence: An acquaintance seen twice a year belongs to a different circle, and the information circulating there is genuinely new.

twice.etymology: 古英語 twiges(二度)。ゲルマン系
twice.usage_in_passage: 接触頻度を数値で示し、"seen rarely" を具体化する。
twice.context_sentence: An acquaintance seen twice a year belongs to a different circle, and the information circulating there is genuinely new.

belongs.etymology: be- + long(古英語 langian 属する)。ゲルマン系
belongs.usage_in_passage: "belongs to a different circle" が、弱い紐帯の価値の源が別の集団への所属にあることを明示する。
belongs.context_sentence: An acquaintance seen twice a year belongs to a different circle, and the information circulating there is genuinely new.

circulating.usage_in_passage: 情報が集団の内部を巡るという運動のイメージを与え、集団間の移動を扱う第3段落へつなぐ。
circulating.context_sentence: An acquaintance seen twice a year belongs to a different circle, and the information circulating there is genuinely new.

genuinely.etymology: ラテン語 genuinus(生来の) → genuine + -ly
genuinely.usage_in_passage: "genuinely new" が、重複でない情報だけが価値を持つという議論の要点を強調する。
genuinely.context_sentence: An acquaintance seen twice a year belongs to a different circle, and the information circulating there is genuinely new.

depends.etymology: ラテン語 de-(下に) + pendere(吊るす) → dependere「ぶら下がる」
depends.usage_in_passage: "depends less on its warmth than on the distance it spans" が本文の中心命題で、評価軸の置き換えを宣言する。
depends.context_sentence: The value of a relationship as a channel depends less on its warmth than on the distance it spans, and casual ties tend to span the greater distance precisely because they are casual.

warmth.etymology: 古英語 wearm(暖かい) + -th。ゲルマン系
warmth.usage_in_passage: distance と対置され、退けられる旧来の評価軸を代表する語として機能する。
warmth.context_sentence: The value of a relationship as a channel depends less on its warmth than on the distance it spans, and casual ties tend to span the greater distance precisely because they are casual.

spans.etymology: 古英語 spann(手幅)。ゲルマン系
spans.definition: またがる、隔たりを埋める。
spans.usage_in_passage: 関係を距離を渡す橋として捉え直す動詞で、次文の span と合わせて本文の核心的比喩を成す。
spans.context_sentence: The value of a relationship as a channel depends less on its warmth than on the distance it spans, and casual ties tend to span the greater distance precisely because they are casual.

casual.etymology: ラテン語 casus(偶然、出来事) → casualis
casual.definition: 何気ない、形式ばらない。
casual.usage_in_passage: 同一文で二度用いられ、"casual ties tend to span the greater distance precisely because they are casual" という循環的に見えて実は因果を述べる構文を作る。
casual.context_sentence: The value of a relationship as a channel depends less on its warmth than on the distance it spans, and casual ties tend to span the greater distance precisely because they are casual.

ties.etymology: 古英語 tēag(結ぶもの)。ゲルマン系 + -s
ties.usage_in_passage: 表題語であり本文の中心概念。強弱という属性とともに、情報の通り道として一貫して扱われる。
ties.context_sentence: The value of a relationship as a channel depends less on its warmth than on the distance it spans, and casual ties tend to span the greater distance precisely because they are casual.

span.etymology: 古英語 spann(手幅)。ゲルマン系
span.usage_in_passage: 動詞として距離を越える働きを示し、関係の価値を長さで測るという本文の枠組みを支える。
span.context_sentence: The value of a relationship as a channel depends less on its warmth than on the distance it spans, and casual ties tend to span the greater distance precisely because they are casual.

precisely.etymology: ラテン語 prae-(前もって) + caedere(切る) → precise + -ly
precisely.usage_in_passage: "precisely because they are casual" が、弱さが欠点ではなく機能の源であるという逆説を強調する。
precisely.context_sentence: The value of a relationship as a channel depends less on its warmth than on the distance it spans, and casual ties tend to span the greater distance precisely because they are casual.

consequences.etymology: ラテン語 con-(共に) + sequi(従う) + -ence + -s
consequences.usage_in_passage: "The consequences extend well beyond employment" が第3段落の主題文で、就職という具体例から一般理論へ議論を広げる。
consequences.context_sentence: The consequences extend well beyond employment.

extend.etymology: ラテン語 ex-(外に) + tendere(伸ばす)
extend.usage_in_passage: 議論の適用範囲が拡大することを示し、以降の rumor・technique・contagion の列挙を導く。
extend.context_sentence: The consequences extend well beyond employment.

divided.usage_in_passage: "If a community is divided into dense clusters" が、社会をネットワーク構造として抽象化する条件節を作る。
divided.context_sentence: If a community is divided into dense clusters whose members all know one another, then anything that must travel between clusters, whether a rumor, a technique, or a contagion, can cross only along the sparse links that connect them.

dense.usage_in_passage: sparse と対をなす本文の構造的キーワード。第4段落では貧困地区の網の性質を述べる語として再登場する。
dense.context_sentence: If a community is divided into dense clusters whose members all know one another, then anything that must travel between clusters, whether a rumor, a technique, or a contagion, can cross only along the sparse links that connect them.

clusters.etymology: 古英語 clyster(房)。ゲルマン系 + -s
clusters.usage_in_passage: ネットワーク分析の用語として circle を抽象化し、集団間の橋という議論を可能にする。
clusters.context_sentence: If a community is divided into dense clusters whose members all know one another, then anything that must travel between clusters, whether a rumor, a technique, or a contagion, can cross only along the sparse links that connect them.

rumor.etymology: ラテン語 rumor(うわさ、騒音)
rumor.usage_in_passage: technique・contagion と並置され、構造的制約が内容の性質を問わず働くことを示す三例の一つ。
rumor.context_sentence: If a community is divided into dense clusters whose members all know one another, then anything that must travel between clusters, whether a rumor, a technique, or a contagion, can cross only along the sparse links that connect them.

technique.etymology: ギリシャ語 tekhnē(技術) → technicus → フランス語 technique
technique.usage_in_passage: 有益な情報の代表として、うわさや伝染と同じ経路を通ることを示す。
technique.context_sentence: If a community is divided into dense clusters whose members all know one another, then anything that must travel between clusters, whether a rumor, a technique, or a contagion, can cross only along the sparse links that connect them.

contagion.etymology: ラテン語 con-(共に) + tangere(触れる) → contagio「接触による伝播」
contagion.usage_in_passage: 望ましくないものの例として加わり、構造が価値中立であることを示す。Q4の設問対象となる三例の一つ。
contagion.context_sentence: If a community is divided into dense clusters whose members all know one another, then anything that must travel between clusters, whether a rumor, a technique, or a contagion, can cross only along the sparse links that connect them.

sparse.etymology: ラテン語 spargere(まき散らす) → sparsus「まばらな」
sparse.usage_in_passage: 語彙問題の対象語。dense と対置され、クラスター間をつなぐ数少ない結びつきを指す。第4段落の "the sparse, outward-reaching kind" で議論の結論を担う。
sparse.context_sentence: If a community is divided into dense clusters whose members all know one another, then anything that must travel between clusters, whether a rumor, a technique, or a contagion, can cross only along the sparse links that connect them.

geometry.etymology: ギリシャ語 gē(大地) + metron(測ること) → geōmetria
geometry.usage_in_passage: "The same geometry that makes a bridging tie valuable also makes it fragile" が、価値と脆さが同一の構造から生じるという逆説を数学的な語で表現する。
geometry.context_sentence: The same geometry that makes a bridging tie valuable also makes it fragile, for a connection maintained by neither habit nor affection is the first to lapse when either party grows busy.

valuable.etymology: ラテン語 valere(価値がある) → value + -able
valuable.usage_in_passage: fragile と同一文で対置され、長所と弱点が分離できないことを示す。
valuable.context_sentence: The same geometry that makes a bridging tie valuable also makes it fragile, for a connection maintained by neither habit nor affection is the first to lapse when either party grows busy.

fragile.etymology: ラテン語 frangere(壊す) → fragilis
fragile.usage_in_passage: 橋渡しの紐帯が維持されにくいという実務的な難点を導入し、第4段落の政策論への布石となる。
fragile.context_sentence: The same geometry that makes a bridging tie valuable also makes it fragile, for a connection maintained by neither habit nor affection is the first to lapse when either party grows busy.

neither.etymology: 古英語 nāhwæþer(どちらも〜ない)。ゲルマン系
neither.usage_in_passage: "maintained by neither habit nor affection" が、弱い紐帯を支える力が存在しないことを二重否定で示す。
neither.context_sentence: The same geometry that makes a bridging tie valuable also makes it fragile, for a connection maintained by neither habit nor affection is the first to lapse when either party grows busy.

affection.etymology: ラテン語 ad-(に) + facere(作る) → afficere「心を動かす」+ -ion
affection.usage_in_passage: habit と並び、関係を維持する二つの力として挙げられ、そのどちらも欠くことが脆さの原因だと示す。
affection.context_sentence: The same geometry that makes a bridging tie valuable also makes it fragile, for a connection maintained by neither habit nor affection is the first to lapse when either party grows busy.

lapse.etymology: ラテン語 labi(滑る) → lapsus「滑り落ちること」
lapse.definition: 自然消滅する、途絶える。
lapse.usage_in_passage: 橋渡しの紐帯が意図せず失われる過程を示し、islands という前文の比喩が現実化する経路を与える。
lapse.context_sentence: The same geometry that makes a bridging tie valuable also makes it fragile, for a connection maintained by neither habit nor affection is the first to lapse when either party grows busy.

busy.etymology: 古英語 bisig(忙しい)。ゲルマン系
busy.usage_in_passage: 紐帯が切れる原因を悪意ではなく日常の多忙に帰し、構造の脆さが避けがたいことを示す。
busy.context_sentence: The same geometry that makes a bridging tie valuable also makes it fragile, for a connection maintained by neither habit nor affection is the first to lapse when either party grows busy.

weak.context_sentence: Because weak ties are cheap to maintain, one might conclude that anyone can accumulate them freely, but the circles a person can reach are constrained by where that person already stands.

poverty.context_sentence: Studies of urban poverty have found that residents of isolated neighborhoods are not deficient in social connection; their networks are often unusually dense.
